extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature, philosophy, and history; attendees of a public lecture on hero-worship
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for representing or analyzing heroic figures, myths, and prophets across cultures, with emphasis on sincerity, cultural context, and the kinds of truth myths convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration of Valor
rubrics_metrics.description: Valor celebrated as the central quality that makes man 'become a god' in Norse religion; Odin taught the infinite importance of Valor and his people felt it as a divine message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use valor as a formative principle: valor shows itself 'against the untamed Forests and dark brute Powers of Nature, to conquer Nature for us.' The lecture treats valor as the primary seed-grain of Norse myth, the fountain of pity, truth, and great human qualities. Examples: Odin's exhortation, Thor's labors; tone: robust, homely, and direct rather than theatrical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational seed-idea (single originating concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single essential 'seed' idea underlies and generates a complex mythology or tradition: 'the first seed is the essential thing: any branch strikes itself down into the earth, becomes a new root.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating myths or heroic traditions, aim for a single powerful central image/idea that can organically branch into complexity. Avoid over-engineered collections of unrelated motifs; instead let derivative elements feel grown from a coherent origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust simplicity, veracity, and directness
rubrics_metrics.description: Norse poetic character prizes 'robust simplicity; their veracity, directness of conception.' The style is hearty, homely, and often contains a tint of good humor amid fearful subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain, forceful expression and concrete physical detail ('grasps his hammer till the knuckles grow white') over rhetorical theatricality. Honest, straightforward depiction of feeling and action often reads as more authentic and powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor grounded in earnestness and sadness
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'great broad Brobdignag grin of true humor' that rests on earnestness and sadness is characteristic; mirth must be rooted in a valiant heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mixing humor with tragic or sublime material, ensure the humor arises naturally from the characters' seriousness and struggle rather than undercutting it. Example: Thor's comic episodes (Hymir's caldron, Skrymir) carry a deep underlying earnestness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of pity and gentle beauty amid the terrible
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in grim myth there are 'beautiful traits of pity' and 'the beautiful and gentle' (e.g., Balder the 'white God' and Nanna's thimble) — compassion accompanies valor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance feats and violence with scenes of tenderness or loss; such contrasts deepen the moral and emotional resonance of heroic narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of allegory/playful mythus vs prophetic/devout mythus
rubrics_metrics.description: Different mythic modes exist: some tales are allegoric and half-playful, others prophetic and devout. The tone and function differ ('This is of the allegoric period, as we see, and half play, not of the prophetic and entirely devout').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the mode deliberately: allegory permits comic inversion and paradox (Utgard episodes), while prophetic myth must convey solemn vision and destiny (Voluspa, Ragnarok). Mixing modes is possible but must be handled with clarity of purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perennial inward truth as criterion of lasting myth
rubrics_metrics.description: A myth's longevity depends on an inward perennial truth: 'these old Norse songs have a truth in them... all must have that can very long preserve itself by tradition alone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mythic material by whether it articulates deep, broadly resonant human truths (mortality, struggle, courage). Surface novelty without such truth will not sustain long tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as the first characteristic of the Great Man
rubrics_metrics.description: A Great Man's primary characteristic is 'sincerity, a deep, great, genuine sincerity' — not boastful self-declared sincerity, but an inward condition he 'cannot help' having.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a heroic character or prophet, foreground an unquestionable inner conviction and earnestness. Anti-pattern: portrayed 'sincerity' that is merely self-congratulating or conscious of itself; that reads as shallow and unheroic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / first-hand revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic/prophetic figure is 'an original man; he comes to us at first-hand' and his utterances appear as a kind of 'revelation' directly from the 'Inner Fact of things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize great figures as having access to—or being compelled by—some direct apprehension of reality, rather than relying on hearsay. Voice should feel singular and authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception shapes the hero's social role
rubrics_metrics.description: How a society welcomes a Great Man (as god, prophet, poet, etc.) reveals that age's spiritual condition; 'the manner it has of welcoming a Great Man... is the most significant feature in the history of an epoch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting a hero, show social responses: adulation, deification, prophetic recognition, or neglect—these reactions contextualize the hero and illuminate cultural values. Use reception as interpretive lens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to Nature's laws / practical efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine influential leader or belief must 'conform himself to Nature and the truth of things'—a false man cannot build a lasting religion; 'a false man cannot build a brick house!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make heroic projects plausible by grounding them in believable human motives, constraints, and natural consequences. Grand claims must have credible mechanisms or they risk being dismissed as mere quackery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral struggle and repentance matter more than outward perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward faults do not disqualify greatness if there is 'remorse, temptations, true, often-baffled, never-ended struggle' and repentance—David is 'the truest emblem ever given of a man's moral progress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray heroes as morally complex: allow failings and show authentic inner struggle and repentance. Avoid creating sterilized paragons; narrative depth often comes from persistent moral striving rather than perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and cultural environment shape hero and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment (e.g., harsh Arabian desert, Mecca's Caabah, Bedouin customs) is formative: climate, geography, and social institutions predispose a people to particular forms of religiosity and heroic expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed characters and religious/moral claims in a richly rendered setting that explains their form and urgency. Use local customs, landscape, and social structures to justify character psychology and communal reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reductive skeptical explanations of profound movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The lecture rejects facile explanations that label great religious movements as mere imposture or 'quackery'; the scale and durability of such movements argue for some genuine basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In commentary or fiction, resist simplistic portrayals that reduce a charismatic leader or movement to mere fraud without engaging the experiential, cultural, and existential reasons people followed them. Show why belief made sense to adherents.
